name: Stibnite
toxicityNote: TOXIC: stibnite is antimony sulfide. Do not ingest, make elixirs or handle without washing hands. Keep from children and pets, avoid dust and wear gloves for rough specimens.
physical: Traditionally associated with a feeling of stamina
Crystal healers link it to a grounded, alert feeling
summary: Stibnite is a dramatic silver-grey antimony sulfide in sword-like crystals, a toxic display stone linked to alchemy, transformation and resolve.
intro: Stibnite is one of the most striking minerals ever pulled from a mine. It grows as long, bladed, metallic crystals like silver swords, often fanned out in sprays or clusters, with deep striations and a leaden mirror shine. Japan's Ichinokawa mine and China's Hunan province have produced meter-long crystals. It is extremely soft, about 2, and the blades bend or break easily. It is also toxic, since it is antimony sulfide. Collectors treat it as a showpiece, and crystal practitioners treat it as a display stone associated with powerful transformation.
history: Stibnite's name comes from the Greek stibi, the word for antimony. The mineral has been ground into kohl, a dark eye cosmetic, since ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia. Alchemists were fascinated by antimony, believing it a key to transmutation, and described the metal as a wolf that devours gold. It is the main ore of antimony, which is used in flame retardants, batteries and alloys. Japanese stibnite from Ichinokawa produced some of the most celebrated collector specimens in the nineteenth century. In crystal practice it has a modern reputation as an alchemical stone.
meaning: Crystal practitioners associate stibnite with alchemy, intense change and inner strength. Its sharp, silver blades are linked to the root and third eye chakras, and used symbolically for cutting away what no longer serves you. It is often chosen by people working on shadow integration or major life shifts. Practitioners say it encourages resolve, honest self-assessment and the stamina to see changes through. Emotionally it is associated with steadiness during upheaval and with clear boundaries. Traditionally it is also linked to alertness and strength. Because it is toxic, it is a stone for display only, and not for wearing, carrying or elixirs.
howToUse: Place a stibnite specimen on a shelf or altar as a focus for transformation intentions, and look at it while thinking about one change you are committed to. Keep it behind glass if you have curious children or pets. Wash hands after any handling and use gloves for rough pieces. Avoid carrying it or wearing it. Combine visually with black tourmaline and hematite in a grounded display, but keep the pieces separate.
care: Stibnite is very soft, brittle and toxic. Handle rarely and gently, wash hands afterward, and wear gloves for rough pieces. Never ingest it, never grind it, never place it in water and avoid dust. It tarnishes in humid air, so keep it dry. Cleanse with sound or smoke only. Store in a labeled box away from children, pets and food, and support blades so they do not snap.
identify: Genuine stibnite is lead-grey, metallic, with deeply striated blade-like crystals that may bend slightly and a very soft feel. It is often confused with galena, bismuth and arsenopyrite. Galena forms cubes, and bismuth shows rainbow tarnish. Fakes include painted or coated resin and cast metal. A simple test is hardness: stibnite can be scratched with a fingernail, while many fakes are harder.

faq.a: Yes. Stibnite is antimony sulfide and should not be ingested, ground or put in elixirs. Wash hands after handling, keep it away from children and pets, and use it as a display specimen.
In crystal tradition stibnite is a stone of alchemy, transformation and resolve. People display it on altars or shelves as a focus for big changes and shadow work.

faq.q: Why does stibnite look like swords?
faq.a: Stibnite grows in long, bladed orthorhombic crystals with deep lengthwise striations. These can fan out into sprays that look like silver swords, which is why the mineral is a favorite of collectors.
